derivation:
\section{Deriving the Airy Solution from the Schrödinger Equation}
Assume a linear potential of the form
\[
V(x)=Fx,
\]
where \(F\) is a constant.
The time-independent Schrödinger equation is
\[
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2\psi(x)}{dx^2}
+V(x)\psi(x)=E\psi(x).
\]
Substituting the linear potential gives
\[
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2\psi(x)}{dx^2}
+Fx\psi(x)=E\psi(x).
\]
Rearranging,
\[
\frac{d^2\psi(x)}{dx^2}
-\frac{2m}{\hbar^2}(Fx-E)\psi(x)=0.
\]
\subsection{Introducing a Dimensionless Coordinate}
Define the characteristic length scale
\[
\ell=\left(\frac{\hbar^2}{2m|F|}\right)^{1/3}
\]
and the dimensionless coordinate
\[
z=\operatorname{sgn}(F)\frac{x-E/F}{\ell},
\]
where \(\operatorname{sgn}(F)\) denotes the sign of \(F\).
Since
\[
Fx-E=F\left(x-\frac{E}{F}\right),
\]
we can write
\[
Fx-E=|F|\ell z.
\]
Using the chain rule,
\[
\frac{d}{dx}
=\frac{\operatorname{sgn}(F)}{\ell}\frac{d}{dz},
\]
and therefore
\[
\frac{d^2}{dx^2}
=\frac{1}{\ell^2}\frac{d^2}{dz^2}.
\]
Substituting these expressions into the Schrödinger equation yields
\[
\frac{1}{\ell^2}\frac{d^2\psi}{dz^2}
-\frac{2m|F|\ell}{\hbar^2}z\psi=0.
\]
Multiplying by \(\ell^2\),
\[
\frac{d^2\psi}{dz^2}
-\frac{2m|F|\ell^3}{\hbar^2}z\psi=0.
\]
By the definition of \(\ell\),
\[
\ell^3=\frac{\hbar^2}{2m|F|},
\]
so the equation simplifies to
\[
\boxed{
\frac{d^2\psi}{dz^2}-z\psi=0
}.
\]
\subsection{The Airy Function Solution}
The differential equation
\[
\frac{d^2y}{dz^2}-zy=0
\]
is the Airy differential equation.
Its two linearly independent solutions are
\[
\operatorname{Ai}(z)
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
\operatorname{Bi}(z).
\]
The general solution is therefore
\[
\psi(z)=A\operatorname{Ai}(z)+B\operatorname{Bi}(z),
\]
where \(A\) and \(B\) are constants determined by boundary conditions.
Returning to the original coordinate \(x\), we obtain
\[
\boxed{
\psi(x)=
A\operatorname{Ai}\left(
\operatorname{sgn}(F)\frac{x-E/F}{\ell}
\right)
+
B\operatorname{Bi}\left(
\operatorname{sgn}(F)\frac{x-E/F}{\ell}
\right)
}.
\]
\subsection{Physical Interpretation}
The linear potential has a characteristic length scale
\[
\ell=\left(\frac{\hbar^2}{2m|F|}\right)^{1/3},
\]
which determines the spatial scale over which the wavefunction changes near the point where \(V(x)=E\).
For a linear potential, the Airy solution is exact. The point \(x=E/F\) is also the classical turning point, where the classical kinetic energy vanishes.
The Airy function \(\operatorname{Ai}(z)\) decays exponentially for
\(z\to+\infty\), whereas \(\operatorname{Bi}(z)\) grows exponentially.
Consequently, boundary conditions requiring a decaying wavefunction in
the forbidden region select the \(\operatorname{Ai}(z)\) solution.
A related Airy function appears near a fold caustic in wave dark matter.
There, it describes the interference of merging classical trajectories
and regularises the density divergence predicted by classical mechanics.
